Kafka Streams vs Redis aggregation benchmark

A1 Kafka Streams, streams protocolA2 Kafka Streams, classic protocolB Kafka consumers + Redis

Generated 2026-10-28 05:29 UTC from 68 runs in results/native/runs. Values are median [min–max] (n repetitions); latency is end-to-end from the broker append time of the latest required fragment to the durable PostgreSQL commit, exact percentiles over all actions. “Worst path” is the highest of the INDIVIDUAL, STAGE2 and FINAL paths. Runs with correctness FAIL are excluded from performance summaries.

Recommendation

Basis: result-ready latency (to the moment the result exists, without the persistence step); the end-to-end figures are in the tables above.

No variant met the 500 ms p99.95 SLO in every executed target-load scenario (A1 Streams: FAIL, A2 Classic: FAIL, B Redis: FAIL), so none can be recommended as is for the stated requirement.

Relative to each other, B Redis had the lowest p99.95 in every executed pod-disruption scenario (rolling, abrupt-pod, cold-pod, rescheduling), each time with non-overlapping repetition ranges and at least 10% difference. For the question “which variant processes most reliably under frequent pod rescheduling”, the measured answer on this environment is B Redis; it still exceeds the 500 ms p99.95 SLO, so meeting the SLO requires changes beyond the choice of variant.

Between the two Kafka Streams variants (identical code, different rebalance protocol): A2 Classic was clearly ahead in 2 and A1 Streams in 0 of 4 pod-disruption scenarios (same rule: non-overlapping ranges, ≥ 10%).

A late event is an incoming event whose own durable result (INDIVIDUAL action) committed more than 500 ms after the broker appended it. Late events added = late events among actions in flight during the 120 s after the fault, minus what the same run produces without a fault over that time (S5: per replacement; its recovery time is the slowest of the six). Normal-operation noise (shared PostgreSQL stalls) makes small values imprecise and can make them negative; the > 2 s and > 10 s counts are gross and hardly affected by it. Result ready: the same, measured to the moment the result exists before persistence (pickup; for final aggregates pickup + ML inference). Method and decision use: docs/DISRUPTION-IMPACT.md.

overall: PASS only if the offered load was achieved, correctness passed, and both steady-state and failure-window p99.95 met the SLO; INCONCLUSIVE when the load was not reached, the node was CPU-saturated (p95 > 90%), a window had too few samples, or the run did not drain.

Findings (derived from the data above)

Findings compare only runs with correctness PASS, achieved load and no CPU saturation; the tables above include every run without a correctness failure, so a median here can differ from the table.

  • Best steady-state latency, result ready (S1 p99.95 worst path, ms): B Redis (99.9) ahead of A2 Classic (448.0), difference 78%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest rolling-upgrade latency, result ready (S2 p99.95, ms): B Redis (383.6) ahead of A2 Classic (2,418.1), difference 84%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest abrupt-failure latency, result ready (S3 p99.95, ms): B Redis (9,804.2) ahead of A1 Streams (14,835.5), difference 34%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest cold-replacement latency, result ready (S4 p99.95, ms): B Redis (158.3) ahead of A2 Classic (1,625.5), difference 90%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest rescheduling latency, result ready (S5 p99.95, ms): B Redis (343.6) ahead of A2 Classic (2,341.1), difference 85%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per rollout, result ready (S2): B Redis (0.0) ahead of A2 Classic (23,962.0), difference 100%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per abrupt pod failure, result ready (S3): B Redis (19,685.0) ahead of A1 Streams (43,286.0), difference 55%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per cold pod replacement, result ready (S4): B Redis (0.0) ahead of A2 Classic (6,061.0), difference 100%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Best steady-state latency, end to end (S1 p99.95 worst path, ms): no clear winner — B Redis 1,103.8 vs A2 Classic 1,146.3 (difference 4%; repetition ranges overlap).
  • Lowest aggregation-only latency (S1 p99.95, append → executor pickup, ms): B Redis (41.4) ahead of A2 Classic (394.8), difference 90%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Highest sustained throughput (S1, fragments/s): no clear winner — B Redis 5,958.0 vs A1 Streams 5,949.0 (difference 0%; repetition ranges do not overlap).
  • Lowest rolling-upgrade latency (S2 p99.95, ms): no clear winner — B Redis 1,428.5 vs A2 Classic 2,472.9 (difference 42%; repetition ranges overlap).
  • Lowest failure-induced latency, abrupt pod kill (S3 p99.95, ms): B Redis (9,980.5) ahead of A1 Streams (14,864.4), difference 33%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest failure-induced latency, cold replacement (S4 p99.95, ms): B Redis (1,112.6) ahead of A2 Classic (1,745.3), difference 36%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest latency under frequent rescheduling (S5 p99.95, ms): B Redis (1,276.4) ahead of A2 Classic (2,412.1), difference 47%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per rollout (S2): no clear winner — B Redis -4,109.3 vs A2 Classic 43,582.7 (difference 109%; repetition ranges overlap).
  • Fewest late events added per abrupt pod failure (S3): B Redis (27,037.0) ahead of A1 Streams (48,662.0), difference 44%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per cold pod replacement (S4): no clear winner — B Redis -3,176.0 vs A2 Classic 10,012.0 (difference 132%; repetition ranges overlap).
  • Shortest partition stall after abrupt failure (S3, ms): B Redis (10,409.0) ahead of A1 Streams (15,134.0), difference 31%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Shortest partition stall during rolling upgrade (S2, ms): no clear winner — B Redis 0.0 vs A2 Classic 2,380.0 (difference 100%; repetition ranges overlap).

Recovery reliability

  • A1 Streams: 22 runs, correctness failures: 0; runs whose latency did not return under the SLO within the fault window: 0.
  • A2 Classic: 22 runs, correctness failures: 0; runs whose latency did not return under the SLO within the fault window: 0.
  • B Redis: 24 runs, correctness failures: 0; runs whose latency did not return under the SLO within the fault window: 0.

State size

  • A1 Streams: state-1s: restore 2,809 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 4,444 (n=1) ms; state-10s: restore 2,212 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 3,672 (n=1) ms; state-60s: restore 2,592 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 5,407 (n=1) ms. First tested window where the failure-window p99.95 exceeds 500 ms: state-1s.
  • A2 Classic: state-1s: restore 1 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 1,731 (n=1) ms; state-10s: restore 399 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 1,511 (n=1) ms; state-60s: restore 425 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 3,454 (n=1) ms. First tested window where the failure-window p99.95 exceeds 500 ms: state-1s.
  • B Redis (for comparison): state-1s: failure p99.95 448 (n=1) ms; state-10s: failure p99.95 1,279 (n=1) ms; state-60s: failure p99.95 786 (n=1) ms.

Resource cost (S1)

  • A1 Streams: aggregators 1.26 cores / 2,206 MiB; Kafka broker 0.36 cores / 3,872 MiB.
  • A2 Classic: aggregators 1.06 cores / 2,193 MiB; Kafka broker 0.34 cores / 3,848 MiB.
  • B Redis: aggregators 1.32 cores / 388 MiB; Kafka broker 0.24 cores / 1,557 MiB, Redis 0.28 cores / 1,317 MiB.

Kafka Streams pays for state durability with changelog writes and one standby replica per task (extra broker load and RocksDB memory in the aggregator pods); B pays with a separate Redis server.

Recovery after injected failures

State size and restoration (S6)

Resource consumption (steady)

Limitations of this environment

  • Single OrbStack node: all pods share one VM, one disk and one kernel; node failures, cross-node networking, rack awareness and independent failure domains are not reproduced.
  • The local profile has one Kafka broker and one Redis node; broker failover and Redis replication are only exercised in the HA profile (./scripts/deploy.sh --ha).
  • Other workloads on the same cluster share CPU and memory; runs whose node CPU p95 exceeded 90% are marked INCONCLUSIVE.
  • All timestamps come from the same node clock; cross-machine clock skew is not present here but would be in production.
  • All variants write their actions to one shared PostgreSQL instance on the same VM, so stalls of that write path appear in every variant's end-to-end latency (result-ready and aggregation-only latency exclude it). Result ready omits the publishing step that replaces persistence in production; in A it already includes the transactional Kafka hop to the executor, in B no Kafka publish at all.
  • Steady and failure windows are assigned by the broker append time of an action's source fragment; an action appended shortly before a fault and delayed by it counts as steady. Whole-window figures (used for S2–S5 above) do not depend on this rule; its effect per run is quantified by scripts/analysis/window_sensitivity.py (see docs/ANALYSIS-NOTES.md).

Raw data

Per run: verification.json (all statistics and correctness checks), per_second_latency.csv, lag.csv, throughput.csv, producer.csv, timeline.csv, latencies.csv.gz (every action), resources.json, logs and startup configuration reports. Summary: results/summary.csv.
